recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — the nth term, and what cancels in the third step.
formula_note: This telescoping sum has denominators stepping by 2 (1·3, 3·5, 5·7, …), giving n/(2n+1). A sibling card in this unit steps by 3 instead (1·4, 4·7, 7·10, …), giving n/(3n+1) — the same telescoping method, but check the step size before writing the denominator's coefficient (2 here, 3 there).

steps.label: Find the nth term
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, but never skip it — the denominators are consecutive odd numbers, so find both sequences with the A.P. formula before writing S(n).
lines: (the nth term of an A.P. is a + (n − 1)d)

recall.must_convey: That the two denominators are arithmetic progressions giving 2n − 1 and 2n + 1, so the nth term is 1/((2n−1)(2n+1)).
accept: the denominators are consecutive odd numbers so the nth term is one over two n minus one into two n plus one
both are a p s with common difference two giving two n minus one and two n plus one
use the a p formula on each factor to get the general term
odd numbers kabatti two n minus one and two n plus one vasthai

steps.why: Both factors increase by 2 from term to term, and they always differ by 2. Naming them with the A.P. formula is what turns a visual pattern into an expression you can add.
common_mistakes: Writing the nth term as 1/(n(n+2)), which fits the first term by accident and fails at the second.
Taking d = 1 instead of 2 for a sequence of odd numbers.
steps.memory_tip: Two A.P.s with d = 2: the first gives 2n − 1 and the second 2n + 1. The nth term is their reciprocal product.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. Both sides come to one third.
lines: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 both sides equal 1/3.
accept: left side is one over one times three which is a third and right side is one over three
both sides are one third at n equals one
the first case gives a third on each side
n equals one ki rendu sides one by three

steps.why: A one-line check, but it is the starting point of the proof, and it carries a full mark.
common_mistakes: Writing the right side as 1/2 by forgetting to substitute n = 1 fully.
steps.memory_tip: Both sides come to one third.
lines_compact: ∴ L.H.S = R.H.S, so S(1) is true.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume the statement for one value k and NUMBER the line (1) — Step 3 quotes it, so it has to be labelled.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

lines.text: (take S(k) as true for one natural number k)

recall.must_convey: That S(k) is ASSUMED true for some k in N, written out as the sum up to k terms equals k/(2k+1), and labelled (1) for later use.
accept: assume the statement is true for k so the sum up to k terms equals k/(2k+1)
suppose s of k holds and call it equation one
take it as true for some k in the naturals and number that line
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one ga rastam
reject: then I assume s of k
let it be true for k

steps.why: This is the assumption the method uses. It is not proved here — it is taken as true for ONE value, and Step 3 shows that it then holds for the next value.
common_mistakes: Assuming the statement for ALL k, which assumes what is being proved.
Not numbering the line, so Step 3 cannot cite it.
steps.memory_tip: Assume for k and number the line (1) so Step 3 can quote it.
lines_compact: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. Add the (k+1)th term, put over a common denominator, and factorise the numerator — 2k² + 3k + 1 is the step that finishes it.
lines: So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

recall.must_convey: That the numerator 2k² + 3k + 1 factorises as (2k+1)(k+1), the (2k+1) cancels, and the result (k+1)/(2k+3) is the formula at k+1 because 2k+3 = 2(k+1)+1.
accept: add the next term over a common denominator the numerator becomes two k squared plus three k plus one which factors as two k plus one into k plus one so the two k plus one cancels
after cancelling you get k plus one over two k plus three which is the formula at k plus one
two k plus three is the same as two into k plus one plus one
numerator factorise chesthe two k plus one cancel avuthundi

steps.why: The cancellation is the main step. If the numerator will not factorise to include (2k+1), the algebra has gone wrong earlier.
common_mistakes: Stopping at (k+1)/(2k+3) without showing it equals the formula at k+1.
Using (2k−1)(2k+1) again as the (k+1)th denominator — replacing n with k+1 gives (2k+1)(2k+3).
steps.memory_tip: Add the (k+1)th term over the common denominator; 2k² + 3k + 1 = (2k+1)(k+1) is what cancels.
lines_compact: So S(k+1) is true whenever S(k) is true.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. Write the sentence — it is one line and it is worth a full mark.

lines.text: (S(1) is true, and S(k) true gives S(k + 1) true,
so S(2), S(3), … are true in turn)

lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That because S(1) is true AND S(k) implies S(k+1), the principle of mathematical induction gives the result for every natural number n.
accept: since s of one is true and s of k implies s of k plus one by the principle of mathematical induction it is true for all n
hence by p m i the statement holds for every natural number
the base case and the inductive step together give it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni natural numbers ki true

steps.why: The two earlier parts prove single statements. Only the principle turns them into a claim about every n, so the examiner marks the sentence that names it.
common_mistakes: Writing only 'hence proved' and never naming the principle.
Claiming it for all real numbers instead of all n ∈ N.
steps.memory_tip: One sentence naming the principle, worth a full mark.
lines_compact: Hence, by the principle of finite

insider_note: Find both APs first: 2n − 1 and 2n + 1. In the step, k(2k+3) + 1 factorises as (2k+1)(k+1), and cancelling that against the denominator is the main step.
